name: Tinosorb S (bemotrizinol)
lead: Bemotrizinol, sold by BASF as Tinosorb S and known by the INCI name bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine, is an oil-soluble organic ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens and daily skincare. It absorbs across the UVB and UVA ranges, with absorption peaks reported near 310 nm and 340-345 nm.[1]

It is used widely in European, Australian and Asian sunscreens, and is often described as photostable. Laboratory work from 2001 reported that adding it to formulations helped stabilise the filters avobenzone and ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate under irradiation.[2] In the United States it has not been part of the over-the-counter sunscreen monograph; a 2023 pharmacokinetic study was published as part of work toward its possible inclusion.[3]
Evidence on the ingredient consists mainly of formulation, photostability and absorption studies rather than trials measuring sunburn or skin-cancer outcomes for the filter alone.

paras: Bemotrizinol is a triazine-based molecule that is insoluble in water and dissolves in oils and emollients, so it is typically placed in the oil phase of emulsions. A Grokipedia summary gives its formula as C38H49N3O5 and a molar mass of about 628 g/mol.[1] Chemical names and numbers beyond this are taken from that reference text, which is AI-generated.

A 2001 study in Photochemistry and Photobiology examined oil-in-water sunscreens and reported that bemotrizinol improved the photostability of avobenzone and ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate, two filters known to lose protection under light.[2] A 2014 study evaluated lipid-nanocarrier and nanoemulsion vehicles for UV filters, including penetration and photostability testing.[4] A 2015 study assessed combinations of UV filters with retinyl palmitate, with and without bemotrizinol, for phototoxic risk using in vitro and in vivo assays.[5]

The 2023 preliminary clinical pharmacokinetic evaluation was conducted because bemotrizinol was being considered for the FDA over-the-counter sunscreen monograph.[3] A review of patients who believed they were allergic to sunscreens concluded that true photoallergy to sunscreen ingredients is rare.[6] Environmental monitoring studies have also looked for UV filters, including this one, in marine settings.[7]

Reference summaries state that the filter has been permitted in the European Union since about 2000 and in Australia, at up to 10 percent.[1] The same source states that, as of late 2025, it had not been approved by the US FDA for OTC sunscreens and that approval was anticipated.[1] Status may have changed since.

Skincare communities that discuss sun protection as part of anti-aging routines often mention European and Asian sunscreens containing Tinosorb S, partly because US products have generally not contained it. The sources available for this article do not include direct forum material.

Human data identified are limited. A 2023 clinical pharmacokinetic study evaluated systemic exposure to bemotrizinol in sunscreen use.[3] A questionnaire and photopatch-testing study of self-described sunscreen-allergic patients addressed photoallergy to sunscreen filters generally.[6] No trials were found that test bemotrizinol alone for appearance outcomes such as photoaging.

card.summary: A photostable broad-spectrum UV filter common in EU and Asian sunscreens, with US availability still pending in the sources reviewed.
card.aka: Bemotrizinol, BEMT, Tinosorb S, Escalol S, Parsol Shield
card.note: Not in the US OTC monograph per the cited sources; status may have changed.

quick.overview:
Tinosorb S is a chemical UV filter that absorbs both UVB and UVA light. It is common in European, Australian and Asian sunscreens and is often discussed in skincare communities as a reason to seek out non-US products.

Research mostly covers formulation behaviour: a 2001 study reported it helped stabilise avobenzone and another filter under light. Trials of the filter alone on appearance outcomes were not found.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs ultraviolet photons and releases the energy as heat, and is described as highly photostable.
quick.risks: Photoallergy to sunscreen filters is described as rare in a 2010 study. A 2023 study measured how much is absorbed, as part of work toward possible US OTC inclusion. Environmental monitoring has detected UV filters in coastal waters.
